niche: Mind Hacks, AI Secrets, Bizarre Body Science & Hidden Power Dynamics

ideas.title: I Can Read Your Mind In 5 Seconds
ideas.angle: An interactive live cognitive challenge where viewers are forced through rapid mental constraints (pick a 2-digit odd number between 10 and 50 where both digits are odd and different). Because 37 is the overwhelmingly dominant statistical cognitive shortcut (cognitive anchoring and availability heuristic), revealing 37 shocks the viewer, triggering an avalanche of comments debating whether it worked and driving massive replay loops.

hook.en: Pick a two digit odd number right now.

ideas.reason: Interactive prediction tests consistently drive the highest engagement rates on Shorts. Rapid calculation rules narrow the brain's selection paths without the viewer noticing, leading over 65% of people straight to 37. The instantaneous reveal forces comments ('get out of my head') and repeated views to test friends.
sources: Kubovy, M. & Psotka, J. (1976) 'The predominance of seven and the apparent randomness of spontaneous choices', Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
Gardner, M. (1956) 'Mathematics, Magic and Mystery', Dover Publications

ideas.title: Look At Their Feet, Not Their Face
ideas.angle: Demonstrates the hidden body language leak of foot orientation: people consciously fake smiles and eye contact, but their feet unconsciously point toward where their brain actually wants to be. If their feet point toward the door or away from you during a conversation, they are subconsciously looking for an escape route, triggering viewers to share real-life stories in the comments.

hook.en: Look at their feet while they talk.

ideas.reason: Micro-behavior decoding hooks have peak Viewed-vs-Swiped-Away ratios because they provide actionable, immediate social superpowers that viewers can test right away in their daily interactions. Nonverbal communication research consistently highlights lower limbs as the most honest body language indicator.
sources: Navarro, J. & Karlins, M. (2008) 'What Every BODY is Saying: An Ex-FBI Agent's Guide to Speed-Reading People', HarperCollins
Ekman, P. & Friesen, W. V. (1969) 'Nonverbal Leakage and Clues to Deception', Psychiatry

ideas.title: The 1-Second Lie Detector Scratch
ideas.angle: Explains the physiological 'Pinocchio effect': autonomic stress from deceiving someone triggers histamine release in nasal tissues, causing an involuntary micro-itch or tap on the nose. Viewers learn to detect this micro-behavior instantly, compelling them to comment about people they know who do this constantly.

hook.en: Watch their hand when they answer you.

ideas.reason: Deception detection and micro-expression videos tap into survival instincts and social vigilance. Connecting a biological bodily reflex (histamine-induced micro-itching under cognitive load) to everyday social interactions creates a high-re-watch trigger as viewers examine the physical mechanics.
sources: Gómez Milan, E. et al. (2012) 'The Mental Thermography of Deception: The Pinocchio Effect', University of Granada Department of Experimental Psychology
Vrij, A. (2008) 'Detecting Lies and Deceit: Pitfalls and Opportunities', Wiley Series in Psychology of Crime, Policing and Law
